summary: Mobility is near normal with an MF-Index of 72 and PT ridership at about 86% of pre‑pandemic levels. Fuel‑price pressures are high, yet actual fuel savings from the WFH mandate are far below the theoretical ceiling, signalling weak compliance. Targeted policy tweaks are needed to sustain the modest recovery and address sectoral risk imbalances.

signals.detail: The theoretical ceiling of 35.7 million litres saved per week translates to only 334,000 litres actually saved in the first week—a 0.9% capture rate. This gap reveals poor uptake of the WFH mandate and limits any meaningful fuel‑price relief for the economy.

Daily PT trips total 1,235,713, roughly 86% of the 2019 daily average (≈1.43 million). The ridership component of the MF‑Index (72.7) indicates a solid rebound, though not yet fully back to pre‑pandemic levels.

High‑mobility sectors—Retail & Services, Logistics, Construction—show mobility scores above 85 with WFH adoption below 15%, exposing the economy to congestion, emissions, and supply‑chain strain. Their combined risk rating is HIGH, warranting immediate mitigation.

WFH adoption is uneven: Public & GLCs enjoy 60% WFH, while Logistics and Construction lag at 8% and 5% respectively. This disparity creates equity concerns, as lower‑income, high‑mobility workers bear disproportionate travel burdens.

Elevated fuel prices (RON95 RM4.67/L, Diesel RM5.27/L) provide a price signal for a shift to mass transit, yet weak fuel‑saving compliance and persistent high mobility in key sectors dilute the effect. A modest modal shift is plausible if reinforced by incentives.

recommendation: Introduce tiered incentives for WFH adoption in high‑mobility sectors, aiming for at least 30% WFH in Logistics and Construction by Q2 2027. Pair this with a weekly fuel‑saving target of 5 million litres and a congestion‑pricing pilot in major corridors to accelerate the shift toward public transport. Expand PT service frequency to capture 90% of pre‑pandemic ridership by end‑2027.
